questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Because `T` is `reified` and the function is inlined, each call site substitutes the real type, so `T::class` is `String::class` and then `Int::class`. `simpleName` gives the short name without the package.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this function?
options: Compile error: cannot check for instance of erased type `T`
It compiles but throws `ClassCastException` at runtime when `T` is checked
It compiles with a warning and always returns `false`
questions.explanation: On the JVM, generic type arguments are erased at runtime, so a plain `T` has no class to check against. Making the function `inline` with `reified T` fixes it, because the real type is then pasted in at each call site.

questions.question: A type parameter can be marked `reified` on a regular, non-`inline` function as long as the function is `private`.
questions.explanation: `reified` only works on type parameters of `inline` functions (and inline properties), whatever their visibility. Inlining is what lets the compiler replace `T` with the concrete type at each call site.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: With a reified `T`, `it is T` becomes a real `is String` / `is Int` check at each call site. `2.5` is a `Double`, not an `Int`, so it is filtered out of the second list. This is how stdlib `filterIsInstance<T>()` works.

questions.question: Given these declarations, what happens with the call `loadUser(orderId)`?
questions.code:
typealias UserId = String
typealias OrderId = String

fun loadUser(id: UserId) { /* ... */ }

val orderId: OrderId = "order-42"
loadUser(orderId)
options: It compiles, because both aliases are just `String`
Compile error: type mismatch, `OrderId` is not `UserId`
It compiles, but throws `ClassCastException` at runtime
It compiles with a warning about mixing aliases
questions.explanation: A `typealias` is only another name for an existing type, so `UserId`, `OrderId` and `String` are the same type to the compiler. To get a real compile-time distinction, use `@JvmInline value class UserId(val value: String)`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Value classes get a generated `toString()` (like a data class) and `equals()` that compares the wrapped value. So two `Id(1)` instances are equal even though they are created separately.

questions.question: Which value class declaration compiles on the JVM?
options: `@JvmInline value class Name(val v: String) { val isBlank get() = v.isBlank() }`
`@JvmInline value class Name(var v: String) { val isBlank get() = v.isBlank() }`
`@JvmInline value class Name(val first: String, val last: String)`
questions.explanation: On the JVM a value class needs `@JvmInline` and exactly one read-only `val` constructor property. Extra properties are allowed only if they have no backing field, like the computed `isBlank` getter.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Value classes may have `init` blocks, and they run every time an instance is constructed, so `Email("nope")` fails `require` before `created` is printed. The message comes from the lambda, not the default `Failed requirement.`.

questions.question: Given `@JvmInline value class Price(val cents: Int) : Comparable<Price>`, in which of these uses is `Price` boxed (a real wrapper object allocated)? Select all that apply.
options: Assigned to a variable of the interface type, e.g. `val c: Comparable<Price> = price`
Stored in a local `val price: Price`
questions.explanation: Used as its own non-null type, `Price` is just an `Int` at runtime. It must be boxed when used as a generic type argument, as an interface type, or as `Price?`, because a primitive `int` can't hold null. A value class over a non-null reference type such as `String` is the exception: its nullable form is just `String?`, with no box.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile error: cannot cast to T
questions.explanation: With a reified `T`, `as? T` becomes a real checked `as? Int` / `as? String` cast, so a `String` safely becomes `null`. With a non-reified `T` the cast would be unchecked and the bad value could slip through until it is used.

questions.question: Java code can call a Kotlin `inline fun <reified T : Activity> Context.launch()` helper by passing the type, e.g. `ContextExtKt.<MainActivity>launch(context)`.
questions.explanation: Reified functions only work because the Kotlin compiler inlines the body and substitutes the real type at each call site. Java can't do that, so these functions can't be called from Java. Expose an overload that takes a `Class<T>` instead.

questions.question: Which body completes this common Android helper correctly?
questions.explanation: `Intent` needs a Java `Class<*>`, and `T::class.java` turns the reified `KClass` into one. `T::class` alone is a `KClass`, which `Intent` doesn't accept, and `T.class` is Java syntax.

questions.question: What does this print?
options: Compile error: reified T cannot be a generic type
questions.explanation: You may pass a generic type like `List<String>` as a reified argument, but `T::class` is a `KClass`, and a class has no type arguments. Only `List` and `Map` are left. Use `typeOf<T>()` if you need the full `List<String>`.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: `===` is prohibited for value classes
Prints `true` because both share the interned string "abc"
questions.explanation: A value class has no stable identity, since it may or may not be boxed at any point, so the compiler rejects `===` on it. Use `==`, which compares the wrapped values.

questions.question: Which of these common APIs get the type from a reified type parameter, so you write the type in angle brackets without passing a `Class`? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: `viewModels<VM>()`, Koin's `get<T>()` and `filterIsInstance<T>()` are inline reified functions that read `T::class` internally. The API 33 `getParcelableExtra` takes an explicit `Class<T>`, and `SavedStateHandle.get<T>` is a plain generic that does an unchecked cast.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Unlike `T::class`, `typeOf<T>()` returns a `KType` that keeps type arguments and nullability, including the `?` on `Int?`. Serialization libraries use this to know the full shape of `List<User>`-style types.

questions.question: You need `gson.fromJson<List<User>>(json)` to return real `User` objects. Which extension does that?
options: `inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T = fromJson(json, object : TypeToken<T>() {}.type)`
`fun <T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T = fromJson(json, object : TypeToken<T>() {}.type)`
`inline fun <reified T : Any> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T = fromJson(json, T::class.java)`
`inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T = fromJson(json, List::class.java) as T`
questions.explanation: Inlining with a reified `T` makes the anonymous `TypeToken<List<User>>` subclass capture the full generic type, which Gson reads by reflection. Without `reified`, the token only sees `T`. `T::class.java` (or `List::class.java`) loses the `User` argument, so Gson builds `LinkedTreeMap`s that throw `ClassCastException` later.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `reified` gives you the class, but the list's type argument is still erased at runtime, so `x is T` with `T = List<String>` only checks `is List`. A `List<Int>` passes, which is why checking `T::class` or `is T` against generic types is a classic trap.

questions.question: Java can call the Kotlin function `fun findUser(id: UserId): User`, where `UserId` is a `@JvmInline value class` wrapping `String`, as `findUser("u1")`.
questions.explanation: Functions with value class parameters compile to a mangled JVM name like `findUser-<hash>(String)`. This avoids clashes with a `findUser(String)` overload and stops Java skipping validation. To expose it to Java, annotate it with `@JvmName("findUser")`.

questions.question: A teammate wraps a reified helper in a generic repository function. What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: cannot use `T` as reified type parameter
Prints `String`, since `T` is inferred from `cacheKey`'s call site
questions.explanation: A reified type argument must be a concrete type known at the call site, or another reified parameter. Inside `cacheKey`, `T` is erased, so the compiler refuses. Make `cacheKey` `inline` with `reified T` too.
